title: AI based Network Attack Forecasting from Network Traffic Data
dataset_link:
• Check nciipc.gov.in; helpdesk1@nciipc.gov.in
• Use publicly available datasets such as CIC-IDS2017/2018, UNSW-NB15, CTU-13, CICIoT2023, LANL Authentication Dataset, DARPA Intrusion Detection datasets, together with public knowledge bases such as MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, CVE/NVD and other open cybersecurity resources.
description:
• Background This challenge seeks AI systems capable of learning network behaviour, anticipating attacker progression and supporting proactive cyber defence using the emerging concept of World Models. Design and develop a software prototype that learns the evolving state of a computer network from traffic telemetry and predicts the likelihood and progression of malicious activity before compromise is completed. The solution should ingest network traffic, learn temporal behaviour, forecast future attack states and provide interpretable decision support for defenders. Solutions should demonstrate applicability to enterprise environments and Critical Information Infrastructure.
• Represent network state using feature vectors or graphs.
• Learn state-transition dynamics using sequence models (LSTM, Transformer), Graph Neural Networks, latent state models or other AI techniques.
• Forecast future network states and estimate the probability of attacker progression.
• Map predicted behaviour to recognised attack stages (e.g. MITRE ATT&CK).
• Provide explain ability using attention mechanisms, feature attribution or equivalent techniques • Detailed Description Participants are encouraged to build world models based AI systems that move beyond static intrusion classification towards predictive cyber defence. The solution may utilise flow records, packet captures, authentication logs or other publicly available cybersecurity telemetry. It should model temporal relationships, infer evolving network state, predict future attack progression and present meaningful explanations for its predictions.
Traditional machine learning classifiers applied to network traffic treat each flow in isolation and map it to a binary benign/malicious label. This discards the temporal and causal structure of an infiltration: the sequence in which ports are probed, the pattern in which SYN flags precede ACK floods, the inter-arrival timing of reconnaissance packets before lateral movement begins. An infiltration is a process unfolding over time, not a single anomalous packet.
• World Models - AI architectures that learn an internal causal simulation of how environment states evolve - offer a fundamentally different approach. Rather than classifying traffic, a world model learns the transition dynamics P(S_t+1 | S_t): given the current observed network state (active flows, flag distributions, port activity, packet timing), what is the probability distribution over future states. This enables forward simulation: roll out K steps ahead and identify whether the current trajectory converges to an infiltration state, before the attacker completes the kill chain.
1. Input Data - Two Levels of Traffic Feature Teams must work with both flow-level and packet-level features drawn from open-source network traffic datasets:
• Flow-level features (NetFlow / IPFIX format): source and destination IP/port pairs, TCP flag bitmask (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG), protocol, bytes transferred per flow, packets per flow, flow duration, inter-arrival time (IAT) statistics (mean, variance, max), and bidirectional flow ratios.
• Packet-level features (PCAP-derived): Time-To-Live (TTL) values and their variance across a session, TCP window size, IP fragment flags, payload size distribution, port scan signatures (sequential or randomised port access patterns), and retransmission counts.
The combination of both levels is required because flow-level features capture aggregate behaviour (a SYN flood) while packet-level features expose timing and sequencing patterns (a slow reconnaissance scan designed to evade flow-based thresholds).
2. World Model Architecture The core deliverable is a learned model of network state transition dynamics - not a static classifier. The model must:
• Represent network state as a structured feature vector or graph encoding active flows at time t.
• Learn P(S_t+1 | S_t) - the probability distribution over the next network state given the current state - using a sequence model such as an LSTM, Temporal Transformer, or Graph Neural Network (GNN) operating over time-windowed traffic observations.
• Be trained on labelled open-source datasets using supervised dynamics learning, where ground-truth state transitions are derived from the attack timeline annotations in the dataset.
• Generalise to unseen attack patterns - not merely memorize signatures from the training set.
3. Infiltration Prediction and Attack Stage Mapping The world model must support forward simulation: given current observed traffic, roll out K steps and output
• A time-series probability score: likelihood of infiltration in the next K time windows.
• Predicted attack stage: mapping to MITRE ATT&CK phases - Reconnaissance, Initial Access, Lateral Movement, Command & Control, or Exfiltration - based on the predicted future state.
• Driving features: which specific flags, ports, or flow patterns are contributing most to the infiltration prediction (via attention weights or SHAP values).
The approaches are provided only as examples and are not mandatory. Teams are free to propose alternative architectures that satisfy the objectives.
• Expected Solution(Indicative)
A software-based, fully open-source solution is expected. The solution may include:
• A feature extraction pipeline that ingests CIC-IDS-2018 or CTU-13 CSV flow records and/or raw PCAP files (parsed using Scapy or PyShark) and outputs a timestamped, normalised feature matrix covering both flow-level and packet-level attributes described above.
• A trained world model (LSTM, Transformer, or GNN architecture) that demonstrably learns traffic state transition dynamics - not a static input-output classifier. Training scripts, model weights, and a reproducible training configuration must be included.
• An infiltration prediction engine that performs K-step forward simulation from a current traffic snapshot and outputs: infiltration probability score, predicted MITRE ATT&CK stage, and top contributing traffic features.
• An explainability output for each prediction - using SHAP values or model attention weights - identifying which flags, ports, or flow statistics are driving the prediction. Black-box outputs without interpretability are not acceptable.
• A working demonstration interface (Streamlit, Flask web app, or CLI) that accepts a PCAP or CSV file as input, runs the world model inference, and displays the infiltration probability timeline, flagged flows, and attack stage annotations. The interface must run fully offline without cloud API dependencies.
• Benchmark results comparing model performance (F1 score, precision, recall, false positive rate) against a logistic regression baseline trained on the same features, demonstrating that the world model's temporal dynamics learning provides measurable improvement.
• Expected Solution/Deliverables for Evaluation
• Source Code Link (GitHub/Drive Link)
• Readme with Setup Instructions
• Architecture Document (Max 2 Pages)
• Demo Video (Max 2 Minutes)
• Technical Presentation (Max 5 Slides) .
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, machine learning, predictive applied to a blockchain & cybersecurity problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Blockchain & Cybersecurity. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on api, model, protocol. Sustainability (4/5): has a clear long-term maintenance path. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: AI Based Network Attack Forecasting from Network Traffic Data

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system that learns the normal 'rhythm' of a network from traffic data, then forecasts how an attack would likely progress before it fully compromises anything, mapping predicted behavior to known attack stages so defenders can act proactively instead of reactively.
overview.why_it_matters: Reactive security responds after compromise. Genuine forecasting of attacker progression, using emerging 'world model' AI concepts, gives defenders a real window to act before damage is done.
pain_points: Cyber defense is typically reactive, responding after compromise rather than anticipating it.
No established system learns network behavioral dynamics well enough to forecast attack progression.
Even where prediction exists, interpretability for defenders is often lacking.
overview.background: Proactive cyber defense requires anticipating attacker progression before compromise completes, motivating AI systems that learn network state dynamics using emerging 'World Model' concepts to forecast attack likelihood and progression.
overview.whats_being_asked: A software prototype learning evolving network state from traffic telemetry, forecasting attack likelihood/progression, mapping predictions to MITRE ATT&CK stages, with explainable decision support.
expected_solution: Network state representation (feature vectors or graphs).
State-transition dynamics learning (LSTM, Transformer, GNN, or latent state models).
Attack-progression forecasting mapped to MITRE ATT&CK stages.
Explainability via attention mechanisms or feature attribution.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Very High. Applying 'World Models' (an emerging AI research concept) to cybersecurity attack forecasting is genuinely cutting-edge, research-adjacent territory, real conceptual sophistication.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires real sequence-modeling/graph-ML expertise, MITRE ATT&CK domain knowledge, and explainability techniques together, substantial technical depth.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires genuine advanced ML (sequence models, GNNs) and cybersecurity domain expertise together, a narrow, technically demanding field.

innovation.note: World-Model-based attack forecasting is genuinely novel, research-territory application of an emerging AI concept to cybersecurity.

invention.note: Sequence/graph-based state modeling plus MITRE ATT&CK mapping plus explainability together is substantial technical breadth.

technical_feasibility.note: Public network traffic datasets (with some labeled attack scenarios) exist; the World Model concept itself is achievable via established sequence/graph modeling techniques even without deep theoretical novelty.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly enables proactive rather than reactive cyber defense, genuinely valuable capability shift.

architecture.note: State representation, transition-dynamics modeling, forecast mapping, and explainability together, genuine architectural sophistication.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the higher-scoring PS in this batch, genuinely achievable using established sequence/graph modeling techniques even if the full 'World Model' framing is more conceptual than a rigid technical requirement. Ground your attack-stage mapping explicitly in real MITRE ATT&CK framework structure.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified technical approach options (LSTM, Transformer, GNN) and explicit MITRE ATT&CK mapping requirement give concrete, achievable technical direction.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Building a generic anomaly detector without genuine state-transition forecasting (predicting future states, not just classifying current ones) would miss the actual 'forecasting' ask central to this PS.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Design your model to genuinely forecast future network states (not just classify current traffic), and validate that its predicted progression genuinely correlates with real MITRE ATT&CK attack-stage sequences in your test data.

idea_0_4: Source public network traffic datasets with some labeled attack scenarios (several established cybersecurity research datasets exist).
Design your network-state representation (feature vectors or graph-based) and choose your sequence-modeling approach.
Split: one person on state representation/data pipeline, one on the sequence/transition-dynamics model.
prototype_4_22: Build your network-state representation from traffic data.
Build your state-transition/forecasting model (LSTM, Transformer, or GNN-based).
Start mapping predicted states to MITRE ATT&CK stages.
integration_22_30: Test your model's forecasting against a simulated/labeled attack progression in your test data, confirm it predicts stages before they fully occur, not after.
Build explainability output (attention weights or feature attribution) for predictions.
Refine MITRE ATT&CK stage mapping accuracy.
polish_30_36: Build a clear dashboard showing forecasted attack progression with explainable reasoning and MITRE ATT&CK stage labels.
Rehearse presenting a specific test case where your model forecasted an attack stage before it fully materialized.
Prepare to discuss your model's genuine forecasting capability versus reactive classification.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your model correctly forecasting an upcoming attack stage from your test data before that stage's full traffic pattern actually appears, with the prediction mapped to a specific MITRE ATT&CK stage and explainable reasoning, that genuine forward-looking forecast, not after-the-fact classification, is the actual differentiator this PS is testing for.

strengths: Very well-specified technical approach options and clear MITRE ATT&CK grounding requirement.
Genuinely achievable using established sequence/graph modeling techniques.
weaknesses: Genuine forecasting (versus reactive classification) is a real, easy-to-blur distinction, requires deliberate model design.
Real attack-progression-labeled network traffic data is less common than basic classification datasets.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: ML-heavy, with real MITRE ATT&CK domain grounding for accurate stage mapping.
team_fit.approach: Design explicitly for forecasting (predicting future states) not classification (labeling current states), this distinction shapes your entire model architecture.

ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Correctly mapping predicted network states to real MITRE ATT&CK stages, and designing genuine forecasting (not reactive classification) architecture, that requires real cybersecurity domain knowledge.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded model that classifies current traffic rather than genuinely forecasting future states would miss the PS's actual technical ask, proactive prediction, not reactive detection.

data_resource_availability.status: Public network traffic datasets with some labeled attack scenarios exist for real training and testing.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Construct a synthetic dataset with realistic attack-progression sequences grounded in real MITRE ATT&CK stage patterns if labeled real data is insufficient.

judge_qna.question: How does your model genuinely forecast future attack progression, versus just classifying current traffic as suspicious?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific state-transition modeling approach and show a test case where the model predicted a future stage before that stage's traffic pattern was fully present in the data.
judge_qna.follow_up: How far in advance can your model realistically forecast, and how does confidence change with forecast horizon?

judge_qna.question: How did you validate your MITRE ATT&CK stage mapping is accurate, not just plausible-sounding?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Describe your grounding in real MITRE ATT&CK framework structure and how you validated your model's predicted stages against known attack-progression patterns in your test data.
judge_qna.follow_up: What happens when an attack doesn't follow a standard MITRE ATT&CK progression?
